query: For high-entropy-alloy multilayer protective coatings, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain their resistance to time-dependent plastic deformation? Specify what governs the behavior and why, an unspecified controlled comparison that would reveal it, the expected observations relative to a baseline, applicable boundaries, supporting evidence, and an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In high-entropy-alloy multilayer protective coatings, the resistance to time-dependent plastic deformation is primarily governed by a synergistic mechanism between engineered multilayer interfaces and intrinsic lattice distortions. Specifically, when adjacent high-entropy layers are designed to have moderately negative lattice misfits at their interfaces, these boundaries act as powerful barriers to dislocation motion—mimicking the blocking effects seen in γ/γ′ systems—while the severe chemical disorder in each layer creates strong local lattice distortions that retard dislocation climb and glide. The repeated interruption of dislocations at these tailored interfaces significantly suppresses creep deformation.
generation.material_initial_state: A multilayer protective coating composed of high-entropy alloy layers with a chemically disordered, high lattice distortion structure. Each layer is processed to achieve controlled interfacial lattice misfit (ideally moderately negative) between adjacent layers.
generation.intervention: Engineer the multilayer architecture by adjusting the alloy compositions and layer thicknesses so that the interfaces exhibit a targeted moderately negative lattice misfit. Compare this to a control (monolithic or multilayer with near-zero misfit) produced under identical overall processing conditions.
generation.conditions: Test under high-temperature (e.g., 800–1000 K) and moderate-to-high stress conditions that are typical of service environments where time-dependent plastic deformation (creep) governs performance.
generation.structural_mediator: The artificially tailored coherent or semi-coherent multilayer interfaces exhibiting a moderately negative lattice misfit, combined with the intrinsic lattice distortion within the high-entropy layers.
generation.mechanism: Dislocations generated during high-temperature service are repeatedly pinned or deflected when they encounter the high-energy interfaces produced by a moderately negative misfit. At the same time, the intrinsic chemical disorder yields local strain fields that further impede dislocation glide and climb. The cumulative effect is a substantial reduction in the overall creep rate as dislocation motion is segmented and slowed by the multilayer architecture.
generation.predicted_outcome: The multilayer coating with engineered interfaces will exhibit a significantly lower steady-state creep strain rate, an extended tertiary creep regime, and a longer creep rupture life compared to a homogeneous (monolithic) high-entropy alloy coating or one with non-tailored (nearly zero misfit) interfaces.
generation.baseline: A monolithic high-entropy alloy coating or a multilayer coating fabricated without intentional misfit engineering at the interfaces.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to dominate in temperature and stress regimes where dislocation-mediated creep is the primary deformation mode. At lower temperatures or under extreme stress conditions where diffusion or other mechanisms prevail, the relative benefit of the multilayer interface engineering may diminish.
generation.uncertainty: This hypothesis extends findings from studies on γ/γ′ interfacial effects in high-entropy superalloys (e.g., PMC12842692::web::031::4_conclusions) and the benefits of serrated or engineered grain boundaries in creep resistance (e.g., PMC9848264::web::017::discussion) to the context of multilayer coatings. However, uncertainties remain regarding the quantitative influence of layer thickness, possible interdiffusion between layers, and whether additional mechanisms (such as interface oxidation in service) might interfere with the proposed dislocation blocking.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of protective coatings: (1) multilayer high-entropy alloy coatings with intentionally engineered interfaces to achieve a moderately negative lattice misfit, and (2) control samples either as homogeneous (monolithic) high-entropy coatings or multilayers with nearly zero misfit. Subject both sets to identical high-temperature (800–1000 K) creep tests under controlled mechanical loading.
measurements: Steady-state creep strain rate (via strain–time curves)
Time-to-rupture or creep life under constant stress
Microstructural analysis (TEM/SEM) to quantify dislocation accumulation and verify the presence and characteristics of the engineered interfaces
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the engineered multilayer coatings do not show a statistically significant reduction (e.g., >50% lower creep rate or markedly extended creep life) compared to the control samples, or if microstructural analysis demonstrates that dislocation activity is not impeded at the interfaces, then the proposed mechanistic hypothesis must be rejected.

cited_evidence.text: A clear transition in creep mechanisms is observed, evolving from diffusion-dominated deformation at low stresses to dislocation nucleation, glide, and interaction at intermediate conditions, and ultimately to stress-induced phase transformation at higher stresses and temperatures. This progression is corroborated by atomic-scale structural evolution and steady-state creep theory. Under identical conditions, HESAs show markedly superior creep resistance to HEAs, mainly due to the strong blocking effect of γ/γ′ interfaces on dislocation motion and atomic transport. Both the γ/γ′ lattice misfit and γ′ volume fraction exert a critical influence on creep resistance. The relationship between misfit magnitude and creep behavior is non-monotonic: moderate negative misfit enhances interfacial coherency and stabilizes the microstructure, thereby improving creep resistance, whereas excessively large misfit increases interfacial strain energy and deteriorates performance. A negative misfit is generally more effective in resisting creep because it strengthens the γ/γ′ interface and reduces dislocation transmissibility. Both HT-1 and HT-2 samples have almost identical tensile strength and ductility at 25°C (Table 1 and Figure 6); ductile transgranular fractures were dominant at room temperature (Figure 7(a,c)). However, when testing temperature was increased to 650°C, a significant hot ductility drop was observed for HT-1 sample. According to Figure 7(b), the facet cleavage surface and the limited amount of plastic deformation indicate that the failure mechanism was brittle intergranular fracture. The brittleness of HT-1 sample was even more pronounced under creep at 650°C as the creep fracture strain was only 0.03%. Cleavage edges on crept fracture surface (Figure 9(b)) and crack propagation along straight grain boundary (Figure 10(b)) indicate the vulnerability of straight grain boundary in HT-1 samples at elevated temperature. According to the local strain concentration at triple junctions of grain boundaries (Figure 11(a)), it is probable that HT-1 samples encountered an embrittlement at 650°C. The initiation of creep damage of HT-1 sample was a result of vacancy coalescence on grain boundaries perpendicular to the loading direction and severe strain concentration at grain boundaries.
